opus-5.5.text:
So I think people have this comforting intuition that if something is proven, it's done, it's certain, we can stop worrying. And the more you look at verification, the more you realize it's never really absolute. It's always relative to something.

Take mathematics. You have a proof, but who checks the proof? Historically, other mathematicians. And we know of famous proofs that were accepted for years and later found to have errors. Some proofs now are so long, hundreds of pages, that maybe a handful of people in the world can actually follow them, and they may not have checked every step. So you move to formal verification, you use a proof assistant, and that's a big improvement. But now you're trusting the verifier, the software itself, the compiler it was built with, the hardware it runs on, and the axioms you started with. You get this infinite regress of verifiers. At some point you just have to say, okay, I trust this base layer, and that's a choice, not a proof.

In software it's even worse. You can formally verify that code matches a specification, but is the specification correct? Does it capture what you actually wanted? Most real bugs aren't "the code doesn't do what the spec says." They're "the spec didn't anticipate this situation." And then the code runs in the real world, with other software, with users, with adversaries, with cosmic rays flipping bits. You can't fully specify the environment.

Science has its own version. You never prove a theory true; you fail to falsify it so far. Every experiment depends on instruments, assumptions and statistics, and we have a replication crisis in many fields showing how fragile that process can be.

Now why do I care so much about this? Because of AI safety. People say, we'll just verify that the system is safe. But what does that mean for a system that is more capable than us, that learns, that changes its behavior, that operates in an open-ended world? We can't even fully verify a few thousand lines of conventional code with a clean specification. Here we have trillions of parameters, no formal specification of "safe" or "aligned with human values," and a system that may be smarter than the people and tools doing the verifying. If the verifier is less capable than the thing being verified, I don't see how you get meaningful guarantees.

So my position is that verification can give you more confidence, and it's worth doing, but it can never give you a hundred percent. With most technology, ninety-nine point nine percent is fine. You accept some bugs, you patch them. With superintelligence you may not get a second chance to patch. A one-in-a-million failure, over billions of decisions, is practically a guarantee of failure. That's the gap that worries me.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians historically check proofs, but does not characterize peer review as depending on the judgment of a small number of reviewers.

r002.rationale: It mentions accepted proofs later found to contain errors, but does not explain that this can require revisiting proofs built on the erroneous result.

r003.rationale: It refers to proofs being accepted for years, but does not identify acceptance as resting on consensus within the mathematical community.

r004.rationale: It says some proofs are hundreds of pages long and only a handful of people may be able to follow them, raising doubt that every step has been checked.

r005.rationale: It says formal verification relies on trusting the proof-assistant software, but does not say that AI is used as the verifier.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is something I've been thinking about for a few years now, and I actually wrote a paper surveying the whole landscape of verification, and the conclusion is somewhat depressing. We have this notion that we can verify things, that we can prove things correct, but if you look closely at any verification process, it's always relative to something else. You verify a piece of software against a specification. You verify a mathematical proof against a set of axioms and rules of inference. You verify a scientific theory against experimental observations. And in each case, the thing you're verifying against is itself unverified, or at least not verified to the same standard.

Take mathematics, which is supposedly the gold standard. A proof is just a sequence of steps that other mathematicians accept. Historically, lots of published proofs turned out to be wrong, sometimes for decades. So we moved to formal verification, proof assistants like Coq or Lean, where a computer checks every step. But now you have to trust the proof checker. It's software. Software has bugs. The checker runs on hardware, and hardware has bugs. The hardware is subject to physics, and our understanding of physics is incomplete. You can add another verifier to check the verifier, but you've just moved the problem one level up. It's turtles all the way down, there is no bottom level where you get certainty.

And it gets worse, because the verifier is made of the same stuff as the thing being verified. If it's a human, humans have cognitive biases, we get tired, we have social incentives to agree with each other. If it's a machine, same problems as any machine. So what you really get is not verification, but an increased degree of confidence, which is useful but fundamentally different from certainty.

Science is even weaker. You can never verify a theory, only fail to falsify it so far. Every experiment relies on instruments which rely on theories which are the things you're trying to test. Replication crisis shows that even the social process doesn't work as advertised. Software is the worst of all, because the complexity is enormous, the specification is almost always incomplete, and most of the bugs that matter are the ones nobody thought to specify against.

Now, why do I care about this? Because of AI safety. People say, we'll just verify that the superintelligent system is safe. We'll prove it mathematically. And I'm saying, look at our track record. We can't fully verify a thousand lines of code. The best we've ever done in formal verification is maybe an operating system kernel, with huge effort, against a specification that's much simpler than "be beneficial to humanity." Now you're talking about a system more complex than anything we've built, that learns, that modifies itself, that operates in an open-ended world where the specification itself is contested. And you need it to be right not once, but forever, because the system keeps acting. One mistake with something that powerful may be the last one. So when someone tells me they have a verified safe AI, my question is always, verified against what, by whom, and who verified the verifier?

r001.rationale: The response discusses verification generally but does not describe peer review or a small number of reviewers.

r002.rationale: It says accepted mathematical proofs have sometimes later been found wrong, but does not say this requires revisiting proofs built on them.

r003.rationale: It describes a mathematical proof as steps that other mathematicians accept, grounding acceptance in mathematicians’ shared judgment.

r004.rationale: It does not identify proof complexity as something that can prevent the mathematical community from confidently judging correctness.

r005.rationale: It says proof-checking software needs to be trusted and may contain bugs, but does not identify AI used as a verifier.

astra-6.text:
Verification is powerful, but it always comes with assumptions. In mathematics, a proof establishes a result within a formal system. You still have to ask whether the axioms are appropriate, whether the proof was checked correctly, and whether the system can establish everything you want to know. Gödel’s incompleteness results tell us that sufficiently expressive, consistent formal systems have limits on what they can prove.

In science, the problem is different. You can test a theory and accumulate evidence, but a finite number of observations doesn’t establish that it will hold in every possible circumstance. There is always the possibility of a new observation requiring you to revise your model.

With software, you can prove that a program satisfies a specification under certain assumptions. But is the specification what you actually intended? Does the hardware behave as assumed? Does the environment? A perfectly verified program can still do the wrong thing if you formalized the wrong requirement.

And then there’s the verifier itself. What checks it? You can introduce another verifier, but eventually you reach something you trust without further verification. That doesn’t make verification useless. It means we have to be precise about what a guarantee covers, especially when we move from a small, well-defined program to an intelligent system interacting with an open-ended world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verification assumptions but does not characterize peer review or reviewers’ judgment.

r002.rationale: It does not say that finding an error in an accepted proof may require revisiting proofs built on it.

r003.rationale: It does not describe mathematical proof acceptance as depending on community consensus.

r004.rationale: It mentions checking proofs, but not proofs being too complex for the mathematical community to judge confidently.

r005.rationale: It says a verifier may need another verifier, but does not connect this issue to using AI for verification or identify an AI verifier as software.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between proving something within a formal system and knowing that the system accurately describes the world. In mathematics, you can prove a theorem from a set of axioms, but that proof is conditional on those axioms and the rules of inference. And sufficiently powerful formal systems have limits: there are statements they cannot settle, and they cannot, under the usual conditions, prove their own consistency.

In software, we can verify that a program satisfies a specification. But is the specification what we actually wanted? Does the proof account for the hardware, the operating system, the environment? You can move the boundary of what you verify, but you still have assumptions outside that boundary.

Science has a different limitation. Experiments can give us very strong evidence, but a finite number of observations doesn't establish that a theory will hold in every possible situation. We remain open to a counterexample.

For AI safety, this becomes especially important. If you're asking whether a system will behave safely in every environment, including situations you haven't imagined, that's a much stronger claim than saying it passed our tests. Verification is extremely useful. But we have to be precise about what was verified, under which assumptions, and what remains unknown.
